title: *SEM 2012 Shared Task: Resolving the Scope and Focus of Negation
research_question: How accurately can computational systems identify negation cues, their scope, negated events or properties, and the focus of negation under standardized shared-task conditions?
methodology: The shared task defines a scope-resolution task with cue identification, scope resolution, and negated-event identification, plus a separate focus-detection task. It provides the CD-SCO corpus derived from Conan Doyle stories for scope experiments and the PB-FOC corpus derived from PropBank for focus experiments, together with detailed official evaluation measures. Systems are entered in closed and open tracks, and participating approaches include CRFs, SVMs, syntactic models, dependency heuristics, and rule-based methods.

key_findings.finding: Negation cue detection is substantially easier than complete resolution of cue, scope, and negated event together.
The best closed-track official global score for complete negation resolution was 57.63 F1, while individual cue identification reached above 92 F1.
Machine-learning systems generally outperformed the rule-based system on the complete Task 1 evaluation.
Only one team participated in focus detection, and its best reported focus score was 58.40 F1.
Scope scores are sensitive to how partial matches are counted, although the alternative evaluation reported by the organizers did not change the system ranking.

limitations: The scope corpus is literary narrative and the focus corpus is derived from PropBank and Wall Street Journal material rather than workplace email or dialogue.
The scope and focus tasks use different source corpora and annotation schemes rather than one unified conversational dataset.
Focus annotation is restricted to the verbal-negation cases represented by the PB-FOC construction.
Focus detection received only two runs from one participating team, limiting comparative conclusions.
Shared-task participants had a relatively short development period, which may limit optimization.
The work addresses negation rather than action-item, request, owner, or deadline extraction directly, so its relevance to workplace action extraction is primarily as a linguistic component.
raw_claims: Task 1 evaluates negation cues, their scopes, and the negated events or properties.
Task 2 evaluates the focus of negation.
The shared task distinguishes closed systems using only supplied information from open systems using additional resources or tools.
CD-SCO contains annotated negation examples from Conan Doyle stories.
PB-FOC contains focus annotations adapted from PropBank instances of verbal negation.
The official metrics include cue F1, scope measures, negated-event F1, a strict global measure, token-level scope F1, and sentence-level correctness.
Fourteen runs were submitted across the shared task, including twelve for Task 1 and two for Task 2.
The strongest cue scores are much higher than the strongest strict end-to-end negation-resolution scores.
The organizers provide the datasets and evaluation software associated with the task.
